```plato
//==
// # Collision
//
// Narrow-phase bodies for `collision.types.plato`: the primitive pair tests that
// produce contact points, the manifold that groups them for a body pair, and the
// flattening into the constraint rows `rigid-dynamics.library.plato` solves.
//
// Sections, in order:
//  - Material combination
//  - Contact frames
//  - Primitive pair tests
//  - Manifolds
//  - Constraint rows
//  - Warm starting
//
// CONVENTIONS THAT GOVERN EVERY PAIR TEST HERE, stated once:
//
//   * THE NORMAL POINTS FROM A TOWARD B, where A is the FIRST parameter — the
//     invariant `collision.types.plato` already states for `ContactPoint3D`. The
//     solver reads it as "an impulse of +P along the normal is applied to B and
//     -P to A", so a ball resting on a ground plane, tested as
//     `Collide(ball, ground)`, gets a normal pointing DOWN and is pushed UP.
//     Swapping the arguments of a pair test therefore changes the sign of the
//     result and is not the same call.
//   * PENETRATION IS POSITIVE WHEN THE SHAPES OVERLAP, and is the depth along the
//     normal. Zero is exact touching.
//   * AN EMPTY POINT ARRAY MEANS "NOT TOUCHING". No hit flag and no sentinel: an
//     empty array is this vocabulary's own encoding of "none"
//     (CONVENTIONS.md - Typed indices), and it is also the honest shape for a
//     test like box-versus-plane whose answer is naturally several points.
//   * THE CONTACT POSITION SITS ON THE B-SIDE SURFACE where the two disagree,
//     because that is the surface a penetration is measured back from. The
//     difference is at most the penetration depth and is invisible for shallow
//     contacts, which is the regime a solver is meant to stay in.

library Collision
{
    //==
    // # Material combination
    //
    // Two touching bodies each carry their own friction and restitution; a
    // contact needs one number for each. `PhysicsMaterial` says which rule to
    // apply, per coefficient, and the two materials' rules may disagree — so the
    // pair needs a rule as well as two values. The rule taken is A's: a contact is
    // asked for by one of the two, and letting the FIRST material decide is the
    // only choice that does not need a tie-break rule of its own.

    // The two coefficients merged under one combine rule.
    Combine(kind: MaterialCombine, a: Number, b: Number): Number
        => match (kind) {
            Average => (a + b) * 0.5;
            Min => a.Min(b);
            Max => a.Max(b);
            Multiply => a * b;
        };

    // The dimensionless Coulomb coefficient of a contact between two materials,
    // merged under A's FrictionCombine rule. The DYNAMIC coefficient is the one an
    // impulse solver can use: static friction is a threshold on a force, and an
    // impulse solver has no forces to threshold.
    CombinedFriction(a: PhysicsMaterial, b: PhysicsMaterial): Number
        => Combine(a.FrictionCombine, a.DynamicFriction, b.DynamicFriction);

    // The bounciness of a contact between two materials, merged under A's
    // RestitutionCombine rule.
    CombinedRestitution(a: PhysicsMaterial, b: PhysicsMaterial): Proportion
        => new Proportion(Combine(a.RestitutionCombine, a.Restitution.Value, b.Restitution.Value));

    //==
    // # Contact frames
    //
    // Friction acts in the plane of the contact, so every constraint row needs two
    // unit vectors spanning that plane. Any two will do geometrically; what
    // matters is that the SAME two are used for the life of the row, because the
    // accumulated friction impulse is stored in their coordinates.
    //
    // The tangent is built by crossing the normal with whichever cardinal axis it
    // leans on least, which is never degenerate: a unit vector cannot have a
    // component of magnitude one on two different axes.

    // A unit vector perpendicular to `normal`, chosen by crossing with the
    // cardinal axis the normal leans on least.
    Tangent(normal: Direction3D): Direction3D
    {
        var n = normal.Vector;
        var away = n.X.Abs <= n.Y.Abs && n.X.Abs <= n.Z.Abs
            ? Vector3D(1.0, 0.0, 0.0)
            : (n.Y.Abs <= n.Z.Abs ? Vector3D(0.0, 1.0, 0.0) : Vector3D(0.0, 0.0, 1.0));
        return n.Cross(away).Normalize.FromVectorUnchecked;
    }

    // The second friction direction, completing a right-handed frame with the
    // normal and the tangent. Precondition: the two are unit and perpendicular,
    // which `Tangent` guarantees.
    Bitangent(normal: Direction3D, tangent: Direction3D): Direction3D
        => normal.Vector.Cross(tangent.Vector).FromVectorUnchecked;

    //==
    // # Primitive pair tests
    //
    // Analytic tests over the shapes `stdlib/geometry` already declares. Each
    // returns the contact points of the pair under the conventions in this file's
    // header, and an empty array when the shapes are apart.
    //
    // General convex-versus-convex — GJK for separation, EPA for the penetration
    // depth once the shapes overlap — is NOT here. Both are iterative simplex
    // refinements whose termination is a tolerance choice rather than a formula,
    // which is a piece of work of its own; the primitive pairs below cover the
    // shapes a rigid-body demo actually drops, rolls and stacks.

    // A one-element array when `present` and an empty one otherwise: the array
    // spelling of a maybe. Written as a range of length 0 or 1 rather than as a
    // literal because an EMPTY array literal carries no element type for the
    // checker to read.
    //
    // The value is evaluated either way — Plato is strict, and this is a function,
    // not a conditional — so every caller below must be able to compute a harmless
    // value in the absent case. That is why each pair test guards its divisions
    // rather than relying on the flag to skip them.
    MaybeOne(present: Boolean, value: $T): Array<$T>
        => MapRange(present ? 1 : 0, i => value);

    // A one-element contact array when `present`, empty otherwise.
    MaybeContact(present: Boolean, point: ContactPoint3D): Array<ContactPoint3D>
        => MaybeOne(present, point);

    // A fresh contact point: the solver's accumulated impulses start at zero, and
    // `WarmStartFrom` is what puts a previous frame's values back.
    FreshContact(position: Point3D, normal: Direction3D, penetration: Number): ContactPoint3D
        => ContactPoint3D(position, normal, Length.FromAmount(penetration),
            Impulse.FromAmount(0.0), Vector3D.Zero);

    // The contact between two balls: one point when they overlap, none otherwise.
    // The point sits half a penetration depth inside each surface, the symmetric
    // choice that only the two-sphere case permits. Concentric balls have no
    // separating direction, so the normal falls back to +Z.
    // (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere)
    Collide(a: Sphere, b: Sphere): Array<ContactPoint3D>
    {
        var d = a.Center.Between(b.Center);
        var distance = d.Magnitude;
        var penetration = a.Radius + b.Radius - distance;
        var normal = (distance > 0.0 ? d / distance : Vector3D(0.0, 0.0, 1.0)).FromVectorUnchecked;
        return MaybeContact(penetration > 0.0, FreshContact(
            a.Center + normal.Vector * (a.Radius - penetration * 0.5), normal, penetration));
    }

    // The contact between a ball and an infinite plane, with the ball expected on
    // the plane's POSITIVE side (the side its normal points to). The contact normal
    // is the plane normal REVERSED, because it must run from A (the ball) toward B
    // (the plane); the position is the foot of the ball's centre on the plane.
    Collide(a: Sphere, b: Plane): Array<ContactPoint3D>
    {
        var penetration = a.Radius - b.SignedDistance(a.Center);
        return MaybeContact(penetration > 0.0, FreshContact(
            b.ClosestPoint(a.Center), b.Normal.Vector.Negative.FromVectorUnchecked, penetration));
    }
```
